The model is presented as an interpretive proposition grounded in 46–48 participants’ accounts rather than as a tested causal sequence.

sec.title: 5.6. Comparison with prior work and areas of divergence
sec.p: The present findings are substantially consistent with Rohwer et al. [3] German interview-based study in identifying trust-signaling behaviors and regular relational contact as central to remote leadership effectiveness, and with Kloepfer and Carbon [4] finding, derived primarily from expert and managerial perspectives, that virtual leadership effectiveness requires consciously planned, empathic communicative engagement. However, the present findings diverge from these accounts in cultural specificity: Rohwer et al.’s participants described trust primarily in terms of individual supervisor characteristics without invoking cultural prohibition structures. This divergence is theoretically meaningful rather than incidental: The permission-accumulation process may be substantially more salient in high power-distance contexts than in the low power-distance German settings of Rohwer et al.’s study, suggesting that the cultural context constitutes not merely a moderator but a constitutive element of what remote leadership effectiveness requires and how it is experienced.

The findings are consistent with Mohase et al. [22] finding that psychological safety mediates the relationship between inclusive leadership and employee voice in remote settings, while providing qualitative texture to the mechanisms underlying that mediation. What Mohase et al.’s survey design registers as an inclusive leadership effect may be better conceptualized, in high power-distance contexts, as a permission-accumulation process in which behavioral inclusion gradually overrides a culturally instituted hierarchical prohibition rather than simply strengthening an already available voice disposition. The study is partially inconsistent with accounts in the virtual-team literature that foreground transformational leadership as a particularly promising style for virtual contexts [12]. Participants did not describe their most trusted supervisors in transformational terms; behavioral consistency, not inspirational vision, was the primary trust-generating mechanism they identified.

The theoretical claims advanced here carry different boundary conditions, and these should be stated explicitly. Two mechanisms are proposed as candidates for cross-context transferability: the asymmetric temporal architecture of trust accumulation, which builds on a general negativity-bias regularity in social perception, and the operation of digital micro-behaviors as an always-active signaling domain, which follows from the structural signal impoverishment of remote work rather than from any culturally specific interpretive scheme. Both are nonetheless expected to vary in intensity with platform environments and organizational communication norms. By contrast, the cultural permission structure mechanism is proposed as strongly context-dependent: It presupposes a socialized deference default that is characteristic of high power-distance organizational settings, and the government-versus-technology sector contrast within this sample indicates that even within Indonesia its strength varies with organizational and professional context. Researchers applying these concepts in low power-distance settings should expect the first two mechanisms to be recognizable and the third to be attenuated, transformed, or absent.

sec.title: 5.6.1 Implications for decent work
sec.p: The decent work framing in the title is grounded in the findings as follows. Decent work, as articulated in the International Labour Organization’s Decent Work Agenda [42] and in Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 8 of the United Nations 2030 Agenda [43], encompasses not only employment and income security but also dignity at work, fairness of treatment, and meaningful participation in the decisions that affect working life. The mechanisms identified in this study bear directly on three of these dimensions in remote settings. Participation: The cultural permission structure functions as a systematic constraint on employees’ access to voice, and voice is the primary channel through which remote employees participate in organizational decision-making; where permission is never credibly granted, participation is formally available but substantively foreclosed. Dignity and fairness: The informational asymmetry documented in Theme 2 determines whether remote employees learn of decisions affecting them before or after those decisions are settled, a distinction participants experienced as a marker of respect versus disregard; similarly, the delivery of critical feedback through public versus private channels (Section 4.3.1) directly implicates dignity under face-saving norms. Quality of working life: The asymmetric trust dynamics of Theme 1 mean that sustained supervisory silence degrades not only trust but the experienced security of the employment relationship itself. Remote leadership practice, on this account, is not adjacent to the decent work agenda; the behavioral and system-design conditions specified in this study are among the proximate determinants of whether remote work is experienced as decent work. This connection is developed here rather than treated as incidental framing.

sec.title: 5.7. Practical implications
sec.p: For organizational leaders and managers, the findings suggest a set of leadership behaviors that employees in remote settings perceived as consequential, behaviors that differ substantially from those emphasized in co-located contexts and that merit deliberate cultivation. These include: responding to employee communications with appropriate speed even when a substantive response is not yet possible, thereby counteracting the asymmetric trust-eroding effects of silence; maintaining recognizably consistent communicative personas across formal and informal digital channels; delivering all critical feedback through private rather than group channels, particularly in high power-distance cultural contexts where face threats carry amplified relational costs; modeling the organizational acceptability of uncertainty and error through proactive self-disclosure; and sharing organizationally significant information with employees before rather than after the formal communications process.

The findings also carry implications at the level of organizational system and process design, which should not be reduced to individual leadership behavior. These are interpretive implications derived from employees’ accounts rather than tested system-design interventions; they are offered as design considerations whose effectiveness remains to be evaluated in implementation research. Several of the negative interpretations documented here arise from conditions that organizations can engineer against rather than merely coach against. First, structured communication routines can institutionalize the acknowledgment behaviors that participants read as respect: Explicit organizational response-time norms (including a norm of brief acknowledgment when a substantive response is not yet possible) convert an individual supervisory virtue into a designed system property, reducing the incidence of the diagnostically damaging silences documented in Theme 1. Second, transparent decision records and proactive information-sharing workflows—for example, routinely published summaries of decisions affecting remote staff—directly target the informational asymmetry identified in Section 4.2.2, so that employees’ access to organizationally significant information does not depend on individual supervisory disposition. Third, coordination and workflow platforms shape the visibility conditions under which micro-behaviors are read: Integrated collaboration environments with shared task status reduce employees’ reliance on inferring supervisory attention from latency and presence indicators, whereas fragmented tool ecosystems amplify that reliance. Fourth, channel architecture can be designed to protect face: designating private, low-visibility channels as the default route for critical feedback embeds the face-saving practice documented in Section 4.3.1 into system configuration rather than leaving it to supervisory judgment. In engineering management terms, the interpretive vulnerabilities documented in this study suggest candidate requirements for the design of communication systems and management processes, not only for leadership training, subject to evaluation in the organizational contexts where they would be deployed.

For human resource (HR) professionals and leadership development programs, the findings challenge the assumption that leaders who perform effectively in co-located settings will automatically develop the digital communication competencies required for remote leadership effectiveness. Leadership development programs in Indonesian organizations and more broadly in high power-distance organizational contexts should include specific modules addressing the following areas: digital micro-behavior management and the systematic gap between intended and received signals; the cultural dynamics of face-saving in virtual feedback delivery; the permission-structure mechanism and practical strategies for credibly accelerating it; the asymmetric dynamics of trust accumulation and the disproportionate cost of supervisory silence; and the informational asymmetry of remote settings and the organizational equity implications of how that asymmetry is managed.

For multinational organizations operating in high power-distance Southeast Asian contexts, the findings suggest that leadership development frameworks designed in low power-distance Western organizational cultures cannot be directly transposed. The behavioral competencies that constitute effective remote leadership are culturally mediated: What constitutes an appropriate and effective trust-building or permission-granting signal in an Indonesian context may differ substantially from what employees in European or North American contexts read as similarly consequential. Cross-cultural leadership development should be designed with this interpretive specificity in mind.

For SDG alignment [43], the findings carry direct relevance. SDG 8’s call for productive employment and decent work for all is supported by identifying the specific behavioral conditions—consistency, proactive disclosure, culturally responsive feedback practices, deliberate digital presence management—that enable employees in remote and hybrid settings to exercise meaningful voice and engage fully with their organizational roles. SDG 10’s commitment to reducing inequalities within nations is addressed by surfacing the permission-structure mechanism as a systematic barrier to organizational participation for employees in high power-distance contexts—a barrier that constitutes a form of structural inequality in access to voice, and that specific leadership practices may help mitigate. Organizations and policymakers in Indonesia and comparable Southeast Asian contexts should treat inclusive remote leadership development not as a management efficiency concern but as an equity and decent work imperative. These implications are also consistent with evidence that sustainable leadership in Malaysian higher education depends on context-sensitive implementation, institutional integration, and adaptive leadership practices [44]. Related science-mapping research identifies transformational leadership and knowledge sharing as a growing domain, reinforcing the importance of examining how leadership behaviors shape information exchange and participatory outcomes in digitally mediated workplaces [45].

sec.title: 5.8. Limitations
sec.p: Several limitations require candid acknowledgment. The interpretive design prioritizes analytic depth over distributional representativeness; findings reflect the accounts of 48 employees in specific urban, knowledge-sector, and professional employment contexts, and should not be extrapolated to Indonesian remote workers more broadly without further inquiry. The sample is substantially weighted toward urban, educated, and professional-services-adjacent employment; rural, manufacturing, healthcare, and agricultural sector experiences, which represent the majority of Indonesian employment are entirely absent. This represents a significant boundary condition on the study’s claims, not merely a qualification.

The study relies exclusively on employee self-reports gathered through retrospective interviews, introducing possibilities of recall bias, retrospective sense-making, and social desirability effects. Supervisors’ perspectives are entirely absent, meaning the study captures employee-side perception of leadership rather than the dyadic, mutually constituted construction of leadership meaning. The gap between employee perception and supervisory intent, which this study argues is analytically central cannot itself be examined from a single-perspective design. A related interpretive boundary must be maintained: The findings warrant claims about how leadership behaviors are interpreted by employees and how those interpretations shape workplace responses, not claims about what leaders actually do or intend. A delayed response that an employee reads as inattention may in fact reflect workload, organizational constraint, or system limitations; the contribution of this study lies in explaining the interpretive consequences of such behaviors, not their causes, and conclusions about remote leadership practice should be read within that boundary. A further limitation concerns technological infrastructure. Digital micro-behaviors do not occur in a platform vacuum: A delayed response in an informal messaging application may carry a different meaning from the same delay in a formal project management environment, and organizations with integrated collaboration systems produce different visibility and communication patterns than those relying on disconnected tools. This study did not systematically analyze the platform and infrastructure environments within which participants’ interpretations were formed, and the relationship between digital infrastructure and leadership interpretation is accordingly identified as an important direction for future research rather than an established feature of the present account. The cross-sectional design means that the temporal dynamics of trust accumulation and permission-structure development, which participants described as unfolding over months, cannot be directly observed. Longitudinal interpretive claims should be treated as hypotheses for future investigation rather than established findings. The methodological tension between the study’s inductive orientation and its theoretically organized interview structure (Section 3.3) is a recognized limitation: Despite design features intended to preserve inductive discovery, the possibility of theoretical pre-sensitization cannot be fully excluded.

Negative case analysis identified six participants whose accounts qualified the dominant thematic patterns. P01 and P11 (both technology sector) described hierarchical norms as having substantially weakened in their remote work experience; P06 (Technology, Sumatra) described digital micro-behaviors as largely irrelevant to his trust assessments; P14 (Professional Services) described behavioral inconsistency as a trust signal rather than a trust barrier; and P02 and P09 described preferences for directive hierarchical clarity rather than participative openness. These accounts collectively caution against reading the study’s themes as universally applicable even within the sample. The themes describe dominant patterns across 36–48 participants; the negative cases define their analytical boundaries and scope conditions.

sec.title: 5.9. Future research directions
sec.p: This study opens at least ten productive research directions: (1) Longitudinal qualitative designs tracking trust accumulation and permission-structure development in real time rather than through retrospective accounts. (2) Dyadic qualitative designs incorporating both employee and supervisor accounts to examine the gap between intended and received leadership signals—the asymmetry this study identifies but cannot directly measure. (3) Comparative qualitative studies examining whether the permission-accumulation process operates in similar form in other high power-distance Southeast Asian contexts. (4) Qualitative studies examining digital micro-behavior interpretation in low power-distance contexts to assess cultural specificity of the signaling frameworks identified here. (5) Mixed-methods designs using qualitative findings from this study to develop and validate behavioral measurement instruments for digital communication competence and permission-structure dynamics. (6) Research extending the sample to rural, manufacturing, healthcare, and agricultural sector employees in Indonesian organizational contexts entirely absent from the current study. (7) Experimental research testing whether interventions targeting the specific behavioral competencies identified here produce measurable improvements in psychological safety and voice in Indonesian remote teams. (8) Research examining the role of peer behavior, rather than supervisory behavior alone, in constructing the social proof basis for permission structures. (9) Investigation of gender dynamics in remote leadership perception in high power-distance Indonesian contexts. (10) Systematic examination of sector-level variation in permission-structure dynamics, given that government sector participants described markedly more rigid hierarchical constraints than technology sector participants. (11) Comparative investigation of how digital platform architecture and the integration of organizational collaboration infrastructure condition the interpretation of micro-behavioral signals, connecting the interpretive account developed here to the design of communication and workflow systems in engineering and technology-intensive organizations.

sec.title: 6. Conclusion
sec.p: This inductive qualitative study set out to examine how employees in Indonesian organizations perceive leadership in remote work settings and what meanings they construct from those perceptions in relation to their sense of safety and willingness to engage. The answer that emerged from 48 in-depth interviews, analyzed through RTA, is both empirically grounded and theoretically consequential: Remote leadership is experienced not through formal style categories but through the cumulative texture of behavioral signals transmitted across digital channels. In high power-distance cultural contexts, those signals must be read, verified, and re-verified before the possibility of organizational voice can be genuinely accessed.

Four themes articulate this account. Behavioral consistency—the sustained alignment between what supervisors say and what they do across interactions, channels, and time—functions as the primary trust-generating mechanism in remote settings, operating through an asymmetric accumulation process in which positive gains accrue slowly and negative events, particularly silence, erode them rapidly. Supervisory disclosure of uncertainty, error, and organizational information carries heightened relational weight in digitally mediated settings, where the informational asymmetry between leaders and employees is structurally greater than in co-located environments, and where proactive sharing signals a relational orientation that converts compliance into engagement. The cultural renegotiation of hierarchy in Indonesian organizational contexts is not a passive adjustment to remote work conditions but an active, permission-dependent process in which employees must accumulate specific behavioral evidence that hierarchical norms have been genuinely overridden before voice becomes possible. And the communicative texture of digital presence—the micro-behaviors of camera usage, response latency, channel selection, and status management—constitutes a continuous, largely unintentional leadership signaling domain through which supervisory character, attentional regard, and authentic relational investment are continuously assessed.

An integrated process model of remote leadership interpretation emerges from this account. Digital micro-behaviors constitute the signal input through which employees infer supervisory character. Asymmetric trust accumulation and cultural permission structures then operate as partly parallel and interacting mechanisms: The former concerns perceived reliability and benevolence, while the latter concerns whether upward voice is culturally and organizationally legitimate. Together, these mechanisms condition whether psychological safety becomes available and whether employees engage in voice. This model extends knowledge-based trust theory and negativity-bias findings into remote leadership perception, identifies a signaling domain not captured by conventional communication-quality or LMX accounts, and provides a process-level explanation for how power-distance dynamics shape voice.

The practical implications for leadership development, HR policy, organizational design, and SDG-aligned decent work agendas in Indonesian and comparable Southeast Asian contexts are grounded in employees’ accounts and are offered as actionable starting points. Leadership that remote employees experience as effective is, in participants’ accounts, not reducible to digital skill or platform competence; it involves cultural attunement, behavioral consistency, and deliberate management of the signaling environment that employees inhabit. Organizations that treat remote leadership development as a purely technical challenge rather than a relational and cultural one risk systematically underinvesting in the capabilities that appear to matter most to the employees they seek to lead.

Future research should pursue the longitudinal, comparative, dyadic, and sector-diversified designs that this study’s necessarily bounded scope cannot provide. The conceptual model advanced here from remote leadership behaviors through signal interpretation, trust accumulation, and cultural permission structures to psychological safety and voice is offered as a theoretically grounded and empirically motivated proposition for investigation, not as a conclusion. The findings reported here are consequential; they are also a beginning.
